q-364487.worked_solution:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221930/assets/275b62fbec1c1a550cb23b481ec54c1e12d3d42e70cf95cd917f1b932638add4.png)

The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f({x}_{0})+f({x}_{1})+…+f({x}_{n-1})}})\cdot {{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{ }\text{width}} \\  & =(f(1)+f(1.5)+f(2)+f(2.5))\cdot 0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)=4{x}^{2}-1$ at each left endpoint:

q-19890.name: Question 2
q-19890.problem:
A speedboat travels downstream on a river. The table below gives the speed $v(t)$, in miles per hour, of the boat at certain moments during its journey.

| $t\,(\text{hours})$ | $0$ | $0.5$ | $1$ | $1.5$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $v(t)\,(\text{mi/hour})$ | $10$ | $35$ | $40$ | $65$ | $80$ |

Use a left Riemann sum for $v(t)$ over the interval $[0,2]$ with four subintervals to approximate the total distance traveled by the speedboat.

*Hint: The distance traveled is given by the area under the speed-time graph.*
q-19890.worked_solution:
First, let's compute the step size $Δt,$ which is just the width of each rectangle. In this case, the endpoints of our interval are $a=0$ and $b=2,$ and there are $n=4$ rectangles, so the step size is

$$
Δt=\frac{b-a}{n}=\frac{2-0}{4}=0.5.
$$

The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{v({x}_{0})+v({t}_{1})+…+v({t}_{n-1})}})\cdot \,\,{{Δt}_{⏟}}_{\text{ }\text{width}} \\  & =(v(0)+v(0.5)+v(1)+v(1.5))\cdot Δt.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $v(t)$ at each point:

| $t$ | $0$ | $0.5$ | $1$ | $1.5$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $v(t)$ | $10$ | $35$ | $40$ | $65$ |

Now, we obtain the following approximation for the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(10+35+40+65)\cdot 0.5 \\  & =150\cdot 0.5 \\  & =75\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total distance traveled by the speedboat. So, the distance is $75\,\text{mi}.$

q-86288.name: Question 3
q-86288.problem:
The table below gives the values of a continuous function $f(x)$ over the closed interval $[1,10]$ with a regular step size. Estimate the area under the curve $y=f(x)$ over the interval $[1,10]$ using a left Riemann sum with $3$ equal subintervals.

| $x$ | $1$ | $4$ | $7$ | $10$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $2$ | $0$ | $2$ |
q-86288.worked_solution:
The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f({x}_{0})+f({x}_{1})+…+f({x}_{n-1})}})\cdot \,\,{{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{ }\text{width}} \\  & =(f(1)+f(4)+f(7))\cdot Δx.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the interval $[1,10]$ is divided into $3$ equal subintervals, the width of each subinterval is

$$
Δx=\frac{10-1}{3}=3.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at the left endpoints:

| $x$ | $1$ | $4$ | $7$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $2$ | $0$ |

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(1+2+0)\cdot 3 \\  & =3\cdot 3 \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

q-115676.name: Question 4
q-115676.problem:
A tank is filling with soda. The table below gives the rate $R(t)$, in liters per minute, at which the tank is filling at certain moments since it started.

| $t\,(\text{minutes})$ | $0$ | $3$ | $6$ | $9$ | $12$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $R(t)\,(\text{liters/minute})$ | $30$ | $40$ | $60$ | $70$ | $90$ |

Given that the tank is empty when $t=0,$ use a left Riemann sum for $R(t)$ over the interval $[0,12]$ with four subintervals to approximate the total volume of soda in the tank after $12$ minutes.
q-115676.worked_solution:
First, let's compute the step size $Δt,$ which is just the width of each rectangle. In this case, the endpoints of our interval are $a=0$ and $b=12,$ and there are $n=4$ rectangles, so the step size is

$$
Δt=\frac{b-a}{n}=\frac{12-0}{4}=3.
$$

The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{R({t}_{0})+R({t}_{1})+…+R({t}_{n-1})}})\cdot \,\,{{Δt}_{⏟}}_{\text{ }\text{width}} \\  & =(R(0)+R(3)+R(6)+R(9))\cdot Δt.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $R(t)$ at each point:

| $t$ | $0$ | $3$ | $6$ | $9$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $R(t)$ | $30$ | $40$ | $60$ | $70$ |

Now, we obtain the following approximation for the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(30+40+60+70)\cdot 3 \\  & =200\cdot 3 \\  & =600\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total volume in the tank. So, the volume is $600$ liters.

q-115688.name: Question 6
q-115688.problem:
The table below gives the values of a continuous function $f(x)$ over the closed interval $[-3,3]$ with a regular step size. If the left Riemann sum approximation of the area under the curve $y=f(x)$ with $3$ subintervals defined by the given points has a value of $4$, then what must be the value of $k?$

| $x$ | $-3$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $k$ | $4$ | $5$ |
q-115688.worked_solution:
The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f({x}_{0})+f({x}_{1})+…+f({x}_{n-1})}})\cdot \,\,{{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{ }\text{width}} \\  & =(f(-3)+f(-1)+f(1))\cdot Δx.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $-3$ | $-1$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $k$ | $4$ |

So, we obtain the following approximation to the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(1+k+4)\cdot 2 \\  & =(5+k)\cdot 2 \\  & =10+2k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we are given that $A$ must be $4$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}10+2k & =4 \\ 2k & =-6 \\ k & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

q-86298.name: Question 7
q-86298.problem:
The following table shows the rate of change of a city's temperature over a $10$-hour period, starting at $2\,\text{a.m}.$

| $t\,(\text{h})$ | $2$ | $4$ | $6$ | $8$ | $10$ | $12$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $T\,{(}^{∘}\text{C}/\text{h})$ | $1$ | $k$ | $4$ | $2$ | $3$ | $1$ |

If the left Riemann sum approximation of the total change in the temperature from $2\,\text{a.m}$ to $12\,\text{p.m}$ has a value of $26{\,}^{∘}\text{C},$ what is the value of $k?$
q-86298.worked_solution:
The area $A$ under the curve $y=T(t)$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{T({t}_{0})+T({t}_{1})+…+T({t}_{n-1})}})\cdot \,\,{{Δt}_{⏟}}_{\text{ }\text{width}} \\  & =(T(2)+T(4)+T(6)+T(8)+T(10))\cdot Δt.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $T(t)$ at each point:

| $t$ | $2$ | $4$ | $6$ | $8$ | $10$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $T(t)$ | $1$ | $k$ | $4$ | $2$ | $3$ |

So, we obtain the following approximation to the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(1+k+4+2+3)\cdot 2 \\  & =2(k+10) \\  & =2k+20\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total change in the temperature from $2\,\text{a.m}$ to $12\,\text{p.m}.$ Since we are given that the left Riemann sum approximation of the total change in the temperature is $26{\,}^{∘}\text{C},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2k+20 & =26 \\ 2k & =6 \\ k & =3.\end{aligned}
$$
